results.title: What is Construct Validity? Definition, Types and Examples | Paperpal
results.content: # What is Construct Validity? Construct validity refers to the degree to which a test or measurement assesses what it was designed to measure. To put it simply, construct validity answers the question: “Does this test measure what it claims to measure?” This is especially relevant in evaluating abstract concepts and constructs and is essential for maintaining the integrity of psychological assessments and scientific studies. * **Evidence for construct validity:** Various types of validity can be assessed to accumulate evidence for construct validity, such as face validity (whether a test appears to measure what it is expected to measure), content validity (whether a test measures all dimensions of the construct of interest), criterion validity (whether a test corresponds to a widely accepted measure of the same construct of interest), convergent validity (whether a test correlates positively with measures of similar or related constructs)  and discriminant validity (whether a test does not or shows a weak correlation with measures of unrelated constructs).

I posted about this in r/AskStatistics as well, but im really struggling with understanding the difference between construct and criterion validity. Construct validity is answering the VERY broad question of "is this test/scale appropriately representing the underlying construct that I'm attempting to measure?" Criterion validity, on the other hand, is answering the question of "is this test acting the way it should, given everything I know about the theory in which this construct is based?" Criterion validity is therefore a subset of construct validity. It mentions at the beginning before any validity evidence is discussed that "historically, this type of evidence has been referred to as concurrent validity, convergent and discriminant validity, predictive validity, and criterion-related validity." I think this might be what throwing me off most of all about it since those all are for the most part different things. I'm thinking this is construct validity since it measures the construct equally well for different populations but again, im so shaky on the different types of validity that im not sure if its correct. Everything you mentioned is construct validity. It's not a question of "is it criterion validity or construct validity?" but rather "what aspect of construct validity is being tested?" So think of it less as an "either-or" dichotomy and more of a hierarchy: construct validity is at the top, descending into different types of criterion-related validity (e.g., concurrent, convergent, discriminant, predictive). Criterion validity is akin to setting a cut score on the state bar exam, and then showing that test takers who score above the cut score perform better on an oral exam of jurisprudence administered by a sitting judge. Very simply put construct validity is the degree to which something measures what it claims to measure. Criterion validity is the degree to which something can predictively or concurrently measure something. A test may not measure what it claims too, lacking either divergent or concurrent validity, and a test that accurately measures a latent construct may not have any real predictive validity when deployed in the wild.
